name: Lower trap / serratus work
lead: Lower trapezius and serratus anterior work refers to exercises aimed at the muscles that control the shoulder blade (scapula). The lower trapezius pulls the scapula down and helps rotate it upward, while the serratus anterior pulls it forward around the rib cage; together with the upper trapezius they sustain upward rotation for overhead arm movement.[1][2]

People train these muscles to look better by improving upper-body posture: stronger scapular stabilisers are said to pull the shoulders down and back, counter rounded shoulders and a hunched upper back, and give a broader, more upright look. Lower and mid-trap development also adds visible thickness to the upper back.[4][5]

Wikipedia's article on upper crossed syndrome, the combination of forward head posture and rounded shoulders, describes the middle and lower trapezius as stretched and weak in that pattern, and lists strengthening of the mid and lower back and scapular retractors among suggested approaches, while noting that support for the recommendations is thin.[3] Lifters on T Nation describe the lower traps as often under-trained relative to the upper traps.[6][7]

chain: Shoulder blades sit lower and flatter against the ribcage
angle.text: The aim is to change how the shoulders and upper back sit, so the frame looks more open and upright. Practitioners add rows, wide-grip pulling and similar exercises to routines for rounded shoulders.

paras: The trapezius has upper, middle and lower fibres. The lower fibres arise from the lower thoracic vertebrae and depress and upwardly rotate the scapula, working with the serratus anterior and opposing the levator scapulae and rhomboids.[1]

The serratus anterior arises from the outer surfaces of the upper nine ribs and attaches along the inner border of the scapula, supplied by the long thoracic nerve. It protracts the scapula, nicknamed the boxer's muscle for its role in punching, and its lower part rotates the scapula so the arm can be raised.[2]

The trapezius is described in three parts. The upper fibres elevate the scapula and support the weight of the arm, the middle fibres retract it, and the lower fibres depress it and rotate it. The lower fibres arise from the spinous processes of roughly the fourth to twelfth thoracic vertebrae and insert on the scapular spine, and the muscle is supplied by the accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) [1]. Wikipedia describes the upper fibres as developed by shoulder elevation such as shrugs and cleans, the middle fibres by pulling the shoulder blades together, and the lower fibres by drawing the shoulder blades downward with the arms nearly straight [1].

Damage to the long thoracic nerve is the most common cause of winged scapula, and the nerve is vulnerable in some surgeries such as axillary lymph node clearance.[2] Trapezius dysfunction can cause winged scapula and abnormal scapular movement, and accessory nerve palsy can cause shoulder drooping and pain.[1]

sections.h: Posture, forward head and rounded shoulders
paras: Wikipedia's article on forward head posture describes the head sitting forward of the shoulders, often with rounded shoulders, which it calls upper crossed syndrome; it attributes the rise in neck and upper-back complaints to long periods hunched over laptops, tablets and phones and lists occupations such as dentistry and nursing as associated with hunching [3]. Its proposed mechanism is a chain in which stiff thoracic joints, weakened mid-back muscles and shortened neck extensors combine, and its treatment section describes a combined approach of strengthening the mid and lower back and deep neck flexors, stretching the upper trapezius and mobilising the thoracic spine [3].

The same article carries maintenance notices for original research and insufficient medical references, and several of its claims are flagged as weakly sourced [3]. Readers interested in the look of the shoulder line (a lowered, flatter shoulder blade and a more open chest) will therefore find the anatomical description better established than the training claims.

Descriptions of lower trapezius work generally involve movements that pull the scapulae down and back, such as prone raises and pulldown or row variations, while serratus work emphasises reaching or pressing the scapula forward around the ribcage, as in push-up-plus movements or loaded carries [1][2][5]. In lifting logs, these are folded into warm-ups and accessory work rather than treated as stand-alone routines [4][5][6][7].

Wikipedia's article on upper crossed syndrome lists strengthening middle and lower back muscles, including scapular retractors, as one component of a combined approach alongside stretching tight muscles, thoracic mobilisation and ergonomic changes, and notes that the article's treatment section is flagged as lacking strong sourcing [3]. Reduced strength in the middle and lower trapezius is described there as part of the forward-head, rounded-shoulder pattern [3].

sections.h: Use in posture and lifting communities
paras: Exercises for these muscles appear in posture routines for rounded shoulders and forward-head posture.[3] On T Nation, one user says pulldown variations hit the mid back, rhomboids and lower traps, which he describes as the muscles that bring the scapula into posterior tilt.[4]

Several lifters report a physical therapist telling them that heavy overhead and pressing work had left the upper traps stronger than the middle and lower traps; they describe a fix built around wide-grip pulling work and less overhead pressing.[6][7] Another log describes loaded carries as a way to strengthen the "scapular stabilizers", naming the lower traps.[5]

No studies found on lower trap or serratus strengthening specifically as a posture or appearance intervention. The upper crossed syndrome article cites one randomized trial on thoracic manipulation and neck pain, which is a different intervention.[3]

Anatomical and clinical descriptions of trapezius palsy, winged scapula and scapular dyskinesia exist, but they concern nerve injury and movement disorders rather than cosmetic posture training [1][2]. Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy affects the lower and middle trapezius fibres first, according to Wikipedia [1].

Recent randomized trials of related posture interventions exist. A 2026 trial of 60 adults aged 18 to 40 with text neck syndrome compared conventional therapy with and without Global Postural Re-Education and reported greater improvements in craniovertebral and shoulder angles in the added-re-education group, with the authors cautioning that its sessions were longer [8]. A 2026 trial in 34 patients with nonspecific neck pain compared a video-based home exercise app with a text brochure and found rounded shoulder height improved in both groups without a significant between-group difference [9]. A registered protocol describes a planned trial of telerehabilitation in 56 adults with upper crossed syndrome that will measure craniovertebral and forward shoulder angles and scapular muscle strength [10]. These studies test broader exercise programmes, not lower trapezius or serratus work in isolation.

Scapular exercises sit between rehab, posture and bodybuilding culture. In posture-focused communities they are promoted as a route to open shoulders and a taller-looking stance, and in strength communities they appear as injury-prevention accessories for overhead pressing and the Olympic lifts [5][6][7]. Lifters on T Nation write about shoulder posture in the context of 'flame free' confession and training log threads rather than formal programs [4][5]. The upper trapezius is the visibly prominent part of the neck-shoulder line and is trained by shrugs, while the lower and middle fibres add thickness through the mid-back [1].

timeline.event: A T Nation training log describes loaded carries as work for the lower traps among the scapular stabilisers.[5]
A lifter reports a physical therapist linking heavy overhead work to upper-versus-lower trap imbalance.[7]
A T Nation thread names rhomboids and lower traps as the muscles behind scapular posterior tilt.[4]
Randomized trials and a registered protocol examine posture programmes for text neck, neck pain and upper crossed syndrome.[8][9][10]

lore.intro: On T Nation, lower traps are described as commonly weak relative to upper traps, and lifters share rehab-style pulling work that targets them.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: Weak lower traps and strong upper traps cause shoulders to look elevated or rounded.
claims.believers: Lifters report being told by physical therapists that excess overhead work left upper traps dominant, and one poster describes elevated shoulder blades on a hunched lifter.[4][6][7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes weak, stretched middle and lower trapezius in upper crossed syndrome and notes that its treatment support is thin.[3]

claims.claim: Wide-grip pulling and rows strengthen the lower traps and improve posture.
claims.believers: Posters recommend high-rep, wide-grip cable and pulldown work to rebalance the shoulders.[4][7]
claims.experts: No trials were found testing these exercises for posture or looks.

claims.claim: Lower traps and serratus can make shoulders sit lower and look wider
claims.believers: Lifters describe strengthening scapular stabilisers as improving how the shoulders and upper back sit [5][6].
claims.experts: Anatomy sources describe the lower trapezius as depressing and rotating the scapula [1]; no trial tests whether training changes visible shoulder position.

claims.claim: Strong lower traps and serratus pull the shoulders back and down for a more upright look
claims.believers: Posture-focused lifters and PT-informed posters describe rows, pulldowns and loaded carries as the fix for rounded, elevated shoulders [4][5][7].
claims.experts: Anatomy sources describe the lower trapezius as depressing and rotating the scapula and the serratus anterior as drawing it around the ribcage [1][2]; trials of broader posture programmes have measured shoulder angle changes [8][9].

card.summary: Exercises for the shoulder-blade muscles used in posture routines; anatomy is well described, appearance benefit untested.
card.note: Sources cover anatomy and nerve injury, not training outcomes.

quick.overview:
The lower trapezius and serratus anterior steer the shoulder blade. Posture communities train them to counter rounded shoulders.

Anatomy sources describe their roles; no study found tests this training for posture or looks.
quick.mechanism: The lower trapezius depresses and rotates the scapula and the serratus anterior pulls it around the ribcage, together stabilising it during arm movement.
quick.risks: Low risk in general. Persistent winging or shoulder pain can reflect nerve injury and is a clinical matter.
